opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that the culture removes a lot of the friction between having an idea and actually testing it on a robot. In a lot of places, research moves at the speed of coordination: you write a proposal, wait for resources, negotiate priorities across teams. Here the loop is much tighter. If someone has a hypothesis about data, model architecture, or training recipes, the expectation is that you just go try it, ideally that same week, and let the results do the arguing.

Part of that comes from being small and fairly flat. People aren't siloed into "the hardware person" or "the model person." Researchers spend time with the robots, engineers care about the research questions, and that shared context means fewer handoffs and fewer things getting lost in translation. When everyone understands the whole stack, you can debug much faster, and in robotics most of the time is spent figuring out why something *didn't* work.

There's also a strong sense of focus. A startup can't afford to chase ten directions at once, so there's a lot of discipline about what really matters. For us, the bet is that general-purpose robot foundation models are possible if you get the data and the learning right. Having that north star makes it easier to say no to interesting distractions.

And I'd say there's a certain comfort with being wrong. Robotics is humbling; the real world will tell you very quickly when your idea doesn't hold up. The culture treats failed experiments as information rather than embarrassment, which makes people willing to take bigger swings. Over time, that willingness to iterate quickly and honestly compounds, and I think that's really where the speed comes from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the speed mostly comes from how few layers there are between an idea and a robot actually trying it.

At a lot of places, if you want to test something on hardware, there's a queue, a request, someone who owns the robot, a whole process. At Physical Intelligence the robots are just there. If I have a hunch at ten in the morning, I can have data collected, a model trained on it, and a policy running on an arm by the end of the day, and often someone else has already seen it fail and told me why. That loop is the whole thing. Research speed in robotics is really just how many of those loops you can close per week.

The second piece is that everyone touches everything. There's no sharp line between the people doing data collection, the people writing training code, and the people thinking about the big picture. So when something goes wrong, which in robotics is constantly, the person who notices is usually also someone who can fix it. You don't lose days handing a problem across a boundary.

And then there's a certain tolerance for things being a bit scrappy. We'll run an experiment on a setup that's held together with tape if it answers the question. We care a lot about the result and much less about whether the process looked polished. Physical systems are humbling enough on their own, so nobody is precious about being wrong. You put something out, it breaks, you learn, you go again.

The flip side is that it can be chaotic, and you have to trust people to make good calls without a lot of structure. But for the stage we're at, where the big open questions are still really open, I think that trade is clearly worth it.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest advantage is the short distance between an idea and an experiment. In robotics, you can spend a lot of time debating whether something should work, but putting it on a robot often tells you something you didn’t anticipate. A startup culture can help you get to that feedback faster.

But speed isn’t just about running more experiments. It’s also about sharing what failed, questioning assumptions, and making sure the next experiment actually teaches you something. To me, the best version of that culture combines urgency with patience: urgency about testing ideas, and patience about the research problems that won’t disappear just because you have a deadline.

sol-6.1.text: I think the biggest advantage is the short loop between having an idea and testing it on a robot. In a startup, research and engineering have to stay very close: you try something, see where it breaks, and use that feedback to decide what to do next. That can make progress much faster. But you also have to protect room for longer-term questions, because the experiment that gives you the quickest result isn’t always the one that teaches you the most.
